The clinical summary presents a classic, high-probability case of **progressive massive fibrosis (PMF)** — the most severe form of chronic silicosis. The diagnosis is anchored in three pillars: (1) unequivocal occupational exposure history (20 years in glass manufacturing, a high-risk silica-exposed industry); (2) characteristic and highly specific imaging findings on HRCT — bilateral reticulonodular interstitial fibrosis *plus* eggshell calcifications of mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes, which are virtually pathognomonic for silicosis/PMF; and (3) physiologic impairment consistent with advanced fibrotic lung disease — reduced FEV1/FVC (reflecting architectural distortion and small airways involvement secondary to fibrosis) and *markedly* reduced DLCO (indicating destruction of gas-exchange surface and microvascular loss). The absence of acute or systemic symptoms effectively excludes active infection, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, sarcoidosis (though ACE could be checked, eggshell calcifications strongly favor silicosis over sarcoid), and cardiac pulmonary edema. While pulmonary hypertension is a known complication of PMF and echocardiography is pending, its absence *so far* does not contradict the diagnosis — it is a downstream consequence, not a prerequisite. The case lacks features of other pneumoconioses (e.g., no beryllium exposure, no coal worker’s black lung history, no asbestos-related pleural plaques or asbestosis pattern). Thus, PMF is not just likely — it is the single most coherent, evidence-supported diagnosis.

[EVIDENCE]  
• 20-year occupational silica exposure in glass manufacturing — definitive etiologic risk factor for silicosis.  
• Insidious onset and gradual worsening of exertional dyspnea over 1 year — consistent with progressive parenchymal fibrosis.  
• HRCT shows bilateral reticulonodular interstitial fibrosis — hallmark radiographic pattern of advanced silicosis/PMF.  
• HRCT shows eggshell calcifications of mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes — highly specific imaging sign for silicosis (and less commonly, sarcoidosis or healed TB; but absence of TB symptoms and exposure history makes TB unlikely).  
• PFTs show reduced FEV1/FVC ratio — reflects fibrotic distortion of airways and small airway involvement in PMF.  
• PFTs show markedly reduced DLCO — indicates severe impairment of gas exchange due to parenchymal destruction and capillary loss, typical of PMF.  
• Absence of cough, wheeze, fever, hemoptysis, or systemic symptoms — reduces likelihood of active infection, asthma, or granulomatous diseases with active inflammation.  
• Absence of orthopnea, PND, leg edema, or palpitations — makes decompensated heart failure an unlikely primary driver of dyspnea at this stage.  
• Denial of beryllium exposure — rules out chronic beryllium disease as a mimic.

[GAPS]  
• Echocardiogram results (PASP, RV function) — pending; needed to assess for pulmonary hypertension, a major complication and prognostic determinant in PMF.  
• AFB sputum studies (smear, culture, Xpert MTB/RIF) — not yet reported; required to definitively exclude concomitant tuberculosis, which commonly co-occurs with silicosis and can accelerate progression.  
• Serum ACE level — not specified; though nonspecific, a normal value would further weaken sarcoidosis in the differential.  
• BAL cytology and CD4:CD8 ratio — not performed; could help exclude sarcoidosis or hypersensitivity pneumonitis if diagnostic uncertainty persisted (though imaging makes this unlikely).  
• Prior chest imaging (e.g., old CXR or CT) — not available; would help confirm progression to PMF (by documenting growth of opacities ≥1 cm), but current HRCT findings are sufficient for diagnosis per ILO and ATS guidelines.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF) due to chronic silicosis.
